subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] I dismiss the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of the Philippines.

[2] The Appellant came to Canada in 2014 on a valid work visa. Prior to this, he lived in Papua New Guinea from 2012 to 2014. The Appellant remained in Canada on his work visa which expired in 2018. In 2019, he applied to restore his status but was rejected. He then received a visitor's visa to remain in Canada. In February 2020, he applied for refugee protection.

[3] The Appellant alleges that his wife's family are involved in municipal politics, and he fears that he could be harmed by people who want to get to his wife and her family. He alleges that his wife was threatened in 2010, and in 2015, his brothers told him it was safer to remain in Canada than in the Philippines.

[4] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the claim finding that it was not well-founded. The RPD found the Appellant's evidence was vague and general and did not meet the threshold to establish a serious possibility of persecution or a section 97 risk, on a balance of probabilities.

[5] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred. He argues that electoral violence is a real concern in the Philippines, even if it is decreasing, and that there are increased tensions ahead of the upcoming 2022 elections. He also argues that the Appellant's wife's family could be targeted and therefore so could the Appellant. The Appellant submits two news articles as new evidence.

[6] I find that the RPD's decision is correct. The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant's evidence was vague and general. The Appellant's argument that violence "could" occur does not meet the threshold of a serious possibility of persecution under section 96 or a section 97 risk, on a balance of probabilities. I find the claim is not well-founded.
DECISION

[7] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
NEW EVIDENCE

[8] According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that:
(i) arose after the RPD's decision; or
(ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
(iii) that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

[9] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.2 The Appellant submits two news articles as new evidence. One titled "Philippines seeks to disband private armed groups" is admitted. The other, titled "Philippines: Election related violence leaves 33 dead" is not.

[10] The first article (armed groups) did not appear to have a date on it. However, the Appellant submits that it was from June 30, 2021, and I was able to confirm this on the internet. It therefore post-dates the rejection of the claim and meets the test for subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). It deals with country conditions in the Philippines in terms of political tensions leading up to the 2022 elections and is therefore new and relevant for the claim. It is from a third-party news organization and is credible for admission. I admit this document.

[11] The second article (election related violence) is dated May 14, 2018. It pre-dates the rejection of the claim. The Appellant has not explained why he could not have provided this to the RPD. I recognize that the Appellant did not have counsel at his hearing, but he confirmed that he had counsel who helped him prepare. I therefore find the article does not meet the test for admission under subsection 110(4). Moreover, I find the article provides nothing new as the RPD accepted, based on the record, that election-related violence in the Philippines exists.

subthemes.text:
ANALYSIS

[13] My role is to look at all of the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3 In this instance, I find the RPD's decision is correct.

[14] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about what risk he would face was vague, general and speculative. She accepted that the Appellant's wife's family was involved in politics and that there was a threat made to the wife in 2010 and that the Appellant's brothers told him "Canada is safer" in 2015. The RPD also accepted that there is electoral violence in the Philippines. The RPD also found that the most recent elections had decreased violence from previous elections. Considering all of this evidence in its totality, the RPD found that the Appellant's personal evidence was insufficient to show a forward-facing risk amounting to a serious possibility of persecution. The RPD also considered section 97 of the IRPA, but it found that any risk the Appellant would face would be that of random crime and not a personal risk.

[15] The Appellant argues that, even if there was a reduction in electoral violence, it still exists and includes killings. Moreover, he argues that the new evidence shows that there are tensions increasing with relation to the 2022 elections and that, given that his wife's family are still involved in politics, there is a risk to his life because politicians' family members are often targeted.4 I do not find these arguments persuasive.

[16] First, the Appellant has not pointed to any objective evidence to show that family members of politicians are "often" targeted. The Freedom House report, cited in the National Documentation Package (NDP) and relied upon by the RPD makes reference to "some election-related violence" but does not mention risk to the family members of politicians.5 The article submitted by the Appellant on the possibility of electoral violence talks about particular regions (Mindanao) having higher tensions and does not mention the Appellant's city. It also talks about groups sparking clashes between rival clans and states that armed groups intimidate political rivals.6 The article also mentions general violence at polling places.7 The article does not talk about violence against family members of politicians.

subthemes.text:
[17] Moreover, this article is in line with what the RPD accepted, that there is some risk of electoral violence. This is not in dispute. The RPD's conclusion was that this risk simply did not rise to a serious possibility of persecution for the Appellant. I find this conclusion is correct. While the United Stated Department of State (US DOS) notes that some political families maintain private armies, they also note that this particularly occurs in one region (Mindanao, which is on a different island from where the Appellant is from), and there is no evidence that this is the case where the Appellant's family is in politics (XXXX, Cebu).8 The report mentions the killing of political figures but not their family members.9 The US DOS report also notes that the electoral violence is generally at a higher level of politics than the Appellant's wife's family is involved in.10 The report notes that the municipal (Barangay) elections will next take place at the same time as national elections in 2022; thus, while there is potentially more of a risk of overall violence at this time, this does not establish an increased risk of violence in the Barangay level elections or to the Appellant.11

[18] The RPD considered the fact that the Appellant's wife continued to live in the same place as did her family, and no problems had occurred other than the threat in 2010 and the warning in 2015. Based upon this, the RPD found that the threshold for sections 96 and 97 were not met. It may be that there is some risk of harm due to political violence in the Philippines. However, based on the record before me, I find this is simply a mere possibility and does not rise to the level of a serious possibility of persecution or a section 97 risk, on a balance of probabilities.

I therefore find the article does not meet the test for admission under subsection 110(4). Moreover, I find the article provides nothing new as the RPD accepted, based on the record, that election-related violence in the Philippines exists.

[12] The Appellant asks for an oral hearing. He argues that a hearing should be held because the new evidence supports the Appellant's argument. However, whether the new evidence supports an appellant's position is not part of the test for an oral hearing. The test for a hearing is not met by this evidence. This evidence is about general country conditions and does not raise any serious issue of credibility with regard to the Appellant. I therefore reject the request for an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS
[13] My role is to look at all of the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3 In this instance, I find the RPD's decision is correct.

[14] The RPD found that the Appellant's evidence about what risk he would face was vague, general and speculative. She accepted that the Appellant's wife's family was involved in politics and that there was a threat made to the wife in 2010 and that the Appellant's brothers told him "Canada is safer" in 2015. The RPD also accepted that there is electoral violence in the Philippines. The RPD also found that the most recent elections had decreased violence from previous elections. Considering all of this evidence in its totality, the RPD found that the Appellant's personal evidence was insufficient to show a forward-facing risk amounting to a serious possibility of persecution. The RPD also considered section 97 of the IRPA, but it found that any risk the Appellant would face would be that of random crime and not a personal risk.

[15] The Appellant argues that, even if there was a reduction in electoral violence, it still exists and includes killings. Moreover, he argues that the new evidence shows that there are tensions increasing with relation to the 2022 elections and that, given that his wife's family are still involved in politics, there is a risk to his life because politicians' family members are often targeted.4 I do not find these arguments persuasive.

[16] First, the Appellant has not pointed to any objective evidence to show that family members of politicians are "often" targeted. The Freedom House report, cited in the National Documentation Package (NDP) and relied upon by the RPD makes reference to "some election-related violence" but does not mention risk to the family members of politicians.5 The article submitted by the Appellant on the possibility of electoral violence talks about particular regions (Mindanao) having higher tensions and does not mention the Appellant's city. It also talks about groups sparking clashes between rival clans and states that armed groups intimidate political rivals.6 The article also mentions general violence at polling places.7 The article does not talk about violence against family members of politicians.

[17] Moreover, this article is in line with what the RPD accepted, that there is some risk of electoral violence. This is not in dispute. The RPD's conclusion was that this risk simply did not rise to a serious possibility of persecution for the Appellant. I find this conclusion is correct. While the United Stated Department of State (US DOS) notes that some political families maintain private armies, they also note that this particularly occurs in one region (Mindanao, which is on a different island from where the Appellant is from), and there is no evidence that this is the case where the Appellant's family is in politics (XXXX, Cebu).8 The report mentions the killing of political figures but not their family members.9 The US DOS report also notes that the electoral violence is generally at a higher level of politics than the Appellant's wife's family is involved in.10 The report notes that the municipal (Barangay) elections will next take place at the same time as national elections in 2022; thus, while there is potentially more of a risk of overall violence at this time, this does not establish an increased risk of violence in the Barangay level elections or to the Appellant.11

[18] The RPD considered the fact that the Appellant's wife continued to live in the same place as did her family, and no problems had occurred other than the threat in 2010 and the warning in 2015. Based upon this, the RPD found that the threshold for sections 96 and 97 were not met. It may be that there is some risk of harm due to political violence in the Philippines. However, based on the record before me, I find this is simply a mere possibility and does not rise to the level of a serious possibility of persecution or a section 97 risk, on a balance of probabilities.
CONCLUSION

[19] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
